extracted.intended_audience: student journalists / cub reporters / journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for student reporters on selecting news, organizing beats (runs), gathering tips, conducting interviews, and appropriate diction and style for news writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify opinions and assess audience interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Give reasons for all opinions. How many readers will each story interest? Which stories interest you most? Why? Do some of the stories have more than one kind of news value?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or selecting items, always state reasons for opinions and estimate potential readership and multiple news values that a story may possess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize accuracy over speed
rubrics_metrics.description: Better no story at all than an inaccurate story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work quickly to avoid being scooped but never allow eagerness to lessen accuracy; errors can force corrections, retractions, apologies, or libel damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish expected vs unexpected news
rubrics_metrics.description: News is of two kinds: expected and unexpected. Stories of scheduled meetings, games, plays, etc., are expected news. Stories of accidents, crimes, and other happenings which occur without warning are unexpected news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unheralded events have higher interest values than scheduled happenings of the same importance; reporters should be particularly alert for unexpected occurrences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize and cover 'runs' (beats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the reportorial or 'local' staff are assigned definite 'beats' or 'runs' which they 'cover' each day in search of news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lists principal runs and the kinds of news they yield (Athletic clubs: games/sport gossip; Banks: financial news; Caterers/Florists: society news; Charities/Churches: social/religious work; Civic Organizations: city plans/reforms; City Hall: municipal business; Court House: county business/cases; Doctors/Hospitals/Coroner: epidemics/deaths/accidents; Federal Building/Post Office: federal court/government business; Fire Dept: fires/statistics; High Schools/Colleges: school news; Hotels: visitors/club dinners; Labor: labor conditions/strikes; Lodges: meetings; Markets: market conditions; Police Station/Courts: crime/accidents/trials; Political HQ: political conditions/gossip; Public School Offices: school board decisions; Railroad Offices: wrecks/time schedules; Realty/Title Companies: transfers/failures). The number of reporters per run depends on city size; runs can be subdivided or combined as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep and consult a 'future' (tip) book
rubrics_metrics.description: The city editor keeps a book called the 'future' or 'tip' book containing all sorts of 'tips' or rumors of events which are expected to 'break' at certain times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect tips from reporters, friends, phone contacts, title-company reports, advertisements, rival papers, and street gossip. Use the book to assign and plan coverage of expected events.

rubrics_metrics.name: City editor assigns with clear instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: The city editor makes an assignment sheet, places opposite each tip the name of the reporter who is to handle the story, calls reporters to his desk and gives each his instructions for the day’s work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there are special features to play up, the editor advises specific questions to bring out desired information and tells the reporter where to go. Reporters should understand assignments and seek clarification when in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter must read latest editions of papers
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter must read the latest editions of his own paper and all rival publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preparation avoids repetition of old stories, gives awareness of events on other runs, enables substitution for absent reporters, and alerts the reporter to fresh developments that may yield big stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take clear notes of instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes on Instructions Must Be Clear — the reporter provides himself with a pad of copy paper and a pencil and takes careful notes of the city editor’s instructions to insure himself against overlooking any assignments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask for clarification if in doubt; ensure full understanding before starting the run.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize the run to save steps
rubrics_metrics.description: The skilled news gatherer analyzes his list of assignments and so districts them that he may cover his run with the greatest possible speed and the least travel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan the day's work spatially and temporally to avoid unnecessary back-and-forth; proper organization conserves time and energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the city thoroughly
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurate knowledge of the city is of the greatest importance to the reporter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use maps and directories; when a name/address is not listed, question post-office clerks, mail carriers, laundry drivers, department-store delivery men, policemen, and street-car conductors; do not give up finding people without telephones—go door-to-door in neighborhoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make definite appointments when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Definite Appointments Desirable — the reporter should determine his method of reaching the persons he is to interview; he may make some appointments by telephone but more frequently must go to an address and take chances of obtaining an audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A little careful preparation (appointments) before starting the run will save time and labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate wide acquaintance and 'dark runs'
rubrics_metrics.description: Wide acquaintance among people in all walks of life is of inestimable value to the reporter... He should cultivate 'a few “dark runs”'; that is, sources of news known to him only and productive of tips only on his promise not to divulge his source of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Win confidence of caterers, merchants, professional men, and others; use exclusive contacts to get tips in advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never betray a confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Never betray a confidence. The reporter who 'double crosses' an informant never lasts in newspaper work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict honor in handling confidences keeps sources; betraying trust destroys future access and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ten general requirements for successful interviewing — overview
rubrics_metrics.description: Ten general requirements for successful interviewing are listed (knowledge of the person's career; elementary understanding of the subject; pleasing personality and attractive appearance; ability to ask questions tactfully yet purposefully; instant recognition of news values in statements; power to estimate worth and detect falsehood; skill in selecting characteristic and significant phrases for quotation; ability to draw correct inferences from manner and actions; accurate and retentive memory for details; determination and perseverance to stick to the task).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These ten items define core competencies for effective interviews; a reporter's success is proportional to fulfillment of these requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the person's career before interviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Before he begins an interview, the news gatherer should make sure that he knows the outstanding facts in the career of the person he is to question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preparation prevents embarrassment and supplies live talking points; people warm to interviewers who show intelligent interest in their accomplishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the interview subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding of the subject concerning which the interview is sought is as important as knowledge of the person's career.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn fundamental facts before interviewing (e.g., musical or sporting terminology) so you can ask intelligent questions and understand technical terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versatility is an asset
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors of large city papers send specially trained men on special assignments, but on small papers the reporter must cover a bewildering variety of assignments. Versatility is one of the biggest assets a worker can have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to 'know a little about everything and a great deal about a few things'; prepare by learning basics when assigned unfamiliar topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-reliance and initiative
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-reliance Best — the reporter who would succeed should not ask questions about details he can look up for himself. The good newspaper worker is unsparing of himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do preparatory work independently; do not burden the city editor with tasks you can handle; be willing to work hard for accuracy and interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasing personality and appropriate appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasing personality and attractive appearance aid the reporter in gaining an audience and winning confidence. He should show self-respecting courtesy, be neither servile nor patronizing, and be neatly and quietly dressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid effrontery or over-familiarity; do not flirt or jolly sources into confidence; pay attention to nails, teeth, hair; maintain dignity appropriate to representing the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect worth of information and falsehood
rubrics_metrics.description: Power to estimate the worth of information and to detect falsehood is a required interviewing skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify statements; sift extraneous material; seek corroboration from eyewitnesses and other sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select characteristic phrases for quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Skill in selecting characteristic and significant phrases for quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose memorable, representative quotations that illuminate the subject and avoid trivial or misleading extracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw correct inferences from manner and actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to draw correct inferences from the manner and actions of the person interviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read body language, tone, and context carefully; use such cues to guide follow-up questions but verify any inference through facts or admissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate and retentive memory for details
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurate and retentive memory for details is listed as a requirement for successful interviewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine good memory with careful note-taking to ensure factual precision in reports and quotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination and perseverance in interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination and perseverance to stick to the task, even in the face of downright rudeness, until the desired information is obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be persistent but tactful; maintain professional composure to secure necessary facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use correct audience/spectator terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience is not synonymous with spectators. An audience hears, but spectators only see.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the precise word appropriate to the context (e.g., 'crowd of spectators' for filmgoers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use 'and' for 'to' (avoid colloquial 'try and')
rubrics_metrics.description: Never use and for to. Wrong: I will try and get it for you. Right: I will try to get it for you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard infinitival constructions in news copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish can and may
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember the distinction between can and may. Wrong: Can I take this book with me? Right: May I take this book with me?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'may' for permission, 'can' for ability, in formal news writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer 'dates from' over 'dates back to' for origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use dates back to for dates from. Wrong: His illness dates back to the night... Right: His illness dates from the night...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'dates from' to indicate when something began.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misuse of 'infinite' — prefer 'great' or 'vast'
rubrics_metrics.description: Infinite is a much bigger word than vast or great. Wrong: An infinite number of tourists... Right: A great number of tourists...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve 'infinite' for literal mathematical or philosophical senses; choose 'great' or 'vast' for large quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'fewer' for numbers and 'less' for quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: Less is used of quantity, fewer of numbers. Wrong: There are less students... Right: There are fewer students... Right: There is less room for recreation than usual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply standard fewer/less distinction in copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer 'trousers' over 'pants' in formal usage (regional/style)
rubrics_metrics.description: A man’s nether garments are trousers, not pants. Wrong: The sophomores wear corduroy pants. Right: The sophomores wear corduroy trousers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use regionally and stylistically appropriate garment terms in formal reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never use 'perform' for 'play' (in musical context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Never use perform for play. Wrong: She will perform on the piano. Right: She will play the piano.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'play' for musical performance in typical news copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use 'posted' for 'informed'
rubrics_metrics.description: Posted should not be used for informed. Wrong: He is well posted on current events. Right: He is well informed on current events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose 'informed' in general reporting contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use 'suicide' as a verb
rubrics_metrics.description: Suicide is never a verb. Write committed suicide or killed himself when the verbal idea is to be conveyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: He tried to suicide this afternoon. Right: He tried to commit suicide (or to kill himself) this afternoon. Use 'suicide' as noun when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'refer' not 'allude'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use allude for refer. Wrong: I allude to your statement... Right: I refer to your statement...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'refer' for direct references in reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'awfully' as an intensifier; use 'very' or 'exceedingly'
rubrics_metrics.description: Awfully is one of the worst abused words... use 'very' or 'exceedingly' when the idea of superlative degree is to be conveyed; avoid superlatives in news writing except where they strengthen the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use measured adjectives; avoid gratuitous superlatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'beside' and 'besides'
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between beside and besides. Wrong: Beside his parents he has no relatives. Right: Besides his parents he has no relatives. Right: He will be stationed beside me.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the correct preposition for the intended meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'resemble' not 'favor' (when meaning resemble)
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor should not be confused with resemble. Wrong: She favors her mother. Right: She resembles her mother.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose verbs that accurately convey likeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use 'like' for 'as' or 'as if' in formal writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use like for as or as if. Wrong: I am writing just like I was taught to write. Right: I am writing just as I was taught to write. Right: It looks as if it is going to rain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'as'/'as if' in formal news prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'prior to' for 'before' in simple constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Never use prior to for before. Not good: He worked for my father prior to his appointment... Right: He worked for my father before his appointment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simpler 'before' in clear news writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'rear' rather than 'raise' for bringing up a family (stylistic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ravzse should not be used for rear. Wrong: She raised a large family of boys. Right: She reared a large family of boys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text advises 'reared' in this context; be sensitive to verb choice in idiomatic phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer 'proved' to 'proven' in many contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer proved to proven. Proven is obsolescent. Not good: It has been proven false. Right: It has been proved false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'proved' in formal constructions, per guidance in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'suspect' (verb) not 'suspicion' (misused as verb)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspicion is a noun and should never be used in place of the verb suspect. Wrong: Whom do you suspicion ? Right: Whom do you suspect?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure correct part-of-speech usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use 'witness' when 'see' is intended
rubrics_metrics.description: Witness is a formal verb of narrow legal significance. Weak: We are about to witness a great spectacle. Right: We are about to see a great spectacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve 'witness' for formal/legal contexts; prefer 'see' for ordinary observation.
